nodes.text: Developing and evaluating AI agents that act through software interfaces (code execution, terminal, browser) requires infrastructure that is costly to build and to run at benchmark scale.
As agents become more capable, systematic evaluation before wide deployment matters for identifying and addressing risks.
Multiple existing agent systems (e.g., the WebArena Agent baseline, SWE-Bench and web-browsing baselines reported in the evidence) each target a narrow benchmark family with their own harness.
No single open platform in the evidence integrates a common agent abstraction with a broad set of benchmarks so one agent can be assessed across domains under one framework.

Can one open platform with a common agent-action interface host a single generalist agent that is evaluated, without per-domain prompt changes, across software-engineering, web-browsing, and miscellaneous-assistance tasks, reaching measurable performance in each?
Build such a platform (OpenHands) and evaluate one generalist agent across 15 integrated benchmarks spanning the three task categories.
Provide a minimal common agent-action abstraction, a containerized and reproducibly-tagged runtime, and a deterministic integration-test framework, then attach benchmark harnesses to it.

Run the same CodeActAgent (and a BrowsingAgent variant for web tasks) with no system-prompt modification across SWE-Bench Lite, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, WebArena, MiniWoB++, GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench, MINT, ProofWriter, and Entity Deduction Arena.
On SWE-Bench Lite (300 instances, no hints), CodeActAgent v1.8 reaches 26.0% with claude-3.5-sonnet, 22.0% with gpt-4o, and 6.3% with gpt-4o-mini.
On the HumanEvalFix Python subset (164 instances), CodeActAgent v1.5 fixes 79.3% of bugs in a 0-shot, multi-turn self-debugging setting.
On WebArena (812 instances) and MiniWoB++ (125 environments), BrowsingAgent v1.0 reaches 8.5-15.5% and 40.8% success respectively, depending on the backend model.
On miscellaneous-assistance benchmarks, CodeActAgent v1.5/v1.8 reaches 52.0% on GPQA diamond, 77.3% on MINT math, 78.8% on the challenging ProofWriter subset, and 57.6% on the AgentBench OS subset.

The same unmodified agent produces interpretable results in every task category, consistent with a shared agent interface and one generalist agent being sufficient to obtain cross-domain performance figures; the size of each figure depends strongly on the backend model.

An open, MIT-licensed platform with a minimal agent-action interface, a reproducible runtime, and harnesses for 15 benchmarks, demonstrated with one generalist agent evaluated across all of them without per-domain modification.

Performance is highly sensitive to the backend LLM, most results use reduced-size benchmark subsets for cost reasons, agents still struggle with complex tasks and long-file editing, and building new workflows still requires substantial handcrafted effort. (Limitation IDs L001-L004 in claims/claim_evidence_map.json; this node lists the claims those limitations bound.)

A shared open platform lets researchers compare agents and run systematic, reproducible evaluation across domains rather than building bespoke harnesses, which also supports evaluating risk before deployment.
Improve agents' file-editing performance on long files and explore more automated (e.g., graph-based) workflow construction to reduce handcrafted engineering effort.

An 'agent' here is a loop that observes environment state and emits actions from a small typed set (running code, running a shell command, or interacting with a browser); a 'generalist agent' uses one fixed configuration across task types instead of a per-benchmark configuration.
nodes.audience_note: Adjacent-field readers may know 'agent' only in the RL sense; this defines the software-interaction sense used throughout.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: A generalist agent, unmodified, can resolve a meaningful fraction of real GitHub issues.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: 300 instances, no hint text, 3 backend models compared, to isolate the effect of the backend model from the agent design
experiment_chains.next: establishes the effect on code-editing tasks -> checks whether the same agent transfers to a very different domain (web browsing)

experiment_chains.hypothesis: The same style of agent, adapted to a browsing action, can complete realistic web tasks without domain-specific prompting.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: 812 WebArena instances + 125 MiniWoB++ environments, zero-shot, 3 backend models, to test transfer beyond code
experiment_chains.next: establishes cross-domain transfer -> checks generality beyond code/web to reasoning and tool-use tasks

experiment_chains.hypothesis: The generalist agent's tool use and multi-turn reasoning generalize to graduate-level QA, math with tool feedback, and logical deduction.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: 198-2294 instances across four benchmarks, gpt-4o/claude-3.5-sonnet, to cover reasoning tasks unlike code or web browsing
experiment_chains.next: completes the three-domain narrative that grounds the CONTRIBUTION
